copy:
Every entrepreneur asks me the same question: 'Where do I actually start with AI?'

Not which tool. Not which framework. But which *first step*.

After working with dozens of small businesses, I've found the answer is simpler than you think: start with the problem, not the technology.

Most business owners buy AI tools and work backwards — looking for problems to fit their shiny new solution. Instead, conduct a 1-week time audit. Track every task that feels repetitive, every process that takes longer than it should, every decision that follows a pattern.

Those are your AI opportunities.

In my upcoming book 'AI That Works for Small Business,' I break this down into a 4-phase framework: Assess → Choose → Implement → Optimize.

No jargon. No hype. Just practical steps that work.

What's the one task you'd automate first if you could? Drop it in the comments.

It's understanding *which* problems AI should solve for your business.

Everything else is just noise.

copy:
I grew up in a garage.

Not a Silicon Valley garage where startups are born. A real garage in Michigan, where my father taught me to build boats.

The smell of fiberglass resin. The precision of a hand plane. The lesson that if you cut a board too short, no amount of wishing will make it longer.

Fifty years later, I'm still building. But now I build AI systems, and the lesson is the same: measure twice, cut once.

My memoir 'Tomorrow Is Still Open' traces this journey from that garage through NASA, Silicon Valley, and into the frontiers of artificial intelligence.

It's not really a book about technology. It's a book about curiosity — and what happens when you never stop asking 'why.'

The future of space exploration isn't just about rockets.

It's about human settlements. It's about governance on other planets. It's about whether we repeat our Earthly mistakes or build something better.

My 'Second Generation' series explores these questions through the lens of a lunar colony fighting for independence. It's science fiction, but the questions it asks are very real:

- How do we build laws for places that don't have them yet?
- What does sovereignty mean on a moon base?
- Can we leave our tribalism behind when we leave Earth?

These aren't just story questions. They're engineering questions. Political questions. Human questions.

And they need answering sooner than you might think.

I've learned that the best technology doesn't feel like technology at all.

It feels like magic. Until you understand how it works, and then it feels like... inevitability.

That's how I felt watching the first Moon landing at age seven.
That's how I felt writing my first line of code.
That's how I felt the first time an AI model generated something truly unexpected.

The through line of my career — from NASA to AI — has been the moment when something impossible becomes ordinary.

What's the 'impossible' thing you're working on right now?

copy:
What does it mean to build something that outlasts you?

That question has haunted me since I was old enough to understand mortality. It's why I spent decades in engineering — building things that would fly beyond Earth's atmosphere, that would carry humans farther than any individual could travel.

Now, writing books, I think about it differently.

Ideas outlast hardware. Stories outlast circuits.

My children's generation will inherit both — the physical infrastructure we built and the ideas we encoded. The question is which one will matter more.

In 'Tomorrow Is Still Open,' I imagine the world my grandchildren will inherit: AGI, quantum computing, space colonization. But the real question at the heart of the book isn't about technology at all.

It's about what makes a life worth living when every material problem has been solved.

Five books. One universe.

The No Blue Sky series spans from first contact through lunar colonization to the future of human consciousness.

What started as a single novel about what it means to be human when you're no longer on Earth has become a five-book exploration of:

- First Generation: What do we carry with us when we leave?
- Moon Base One: What does it take to survive?
- Second Generation: What do we owe the children born off-world?
- Third Generation: What happens when Earth is just a story?

Each book builds on the last, asking harder questions about identity, belonging, and what it means to be human when 'home' is no longer a place but an idea.

If you've ever looked at the night sky and wondered 'what if?' — these books are for you.
